machine.title: Keep the machine up and the work safe
machine.covers: The one PC: power-offs, restarts, resuming after a stop, off-machine copies, memory, Docker and disk, and keeping secrets out of agents’ reach.
intro: Everything we build runs on one PC. Between 7 October and 10 November it powered off unexpectedly 24 times [M]. Of the 25 power-offs since 1 October, 15 [M] came with no Claude call in any project in the ten minutes before, so our own load alone does not explain them. Until this month every branch also lived only on this machine.

The ideas here keep work safe when the PC stops and bring it back without me: an off-machine copy, a resume list that brings sessions back two at a time, and an always-on logger that will finally tell us why it powers off. Separate worktrees already pay: when the power went for 28 minutes on 13 November, all eight FixFlow lanes resumed from their own copies [M]. This theme is harness v2 phase 1, and I answered its first six decisions on 11 November; a full restart chain waits, because I chose to keep Docker’s start at sign-in off for now (D03).

check.title: Fast, fair, trustworthy checks
check.covers: The test run that decides whether work is right: speed, the Linux container gate, check slots, fair queues, heartbeats, clean-up, and checks that can really fail.
intro: The check is where our biggest measured wins already are. Running tests in parallel took the clinic check from 855.2 s to 283.8 s [M], tracing start-up took a 16-test run from 43 s to 11.5 s [M], and the Linux container run takes 230.1 s against 367.2 s natively [M].

What remains is making it the one gate everyone trusts: sized from measured memory, fair in its queue, visible while it runs, and never green when it tested nothing. FixFlow’s gate harness already carries several of these ideas into daily use; harness v2 phase 2 does the rest.

review.title: Review and fix rounds that converge
review.covers: Reviewing work and fixing what review finds: fix rounds, claims checks, fresh reviewers, refuters, severity, reading the final commit, and merging.
intro: In the clinic testbed a slice took 2.8 review rounds on average [M], and 64 % of reviews sent the slice back [M]. Some fixes created new defects, some reports claimed more than was done, and in 5 of 6 high-risk merges nobody had read the final commit [M].

The ideas here make review converge and make its verdicts checkable: a contract for each fix round, scripts that test claims, fresh reviewers that try to refute, and a merge queue that records who read what. Harness v2 phase 3 turns the strongest of them into six scripts that spend no tokens.

parallel.title: Planning parallel work
parallel.covers: Running several lanes at once: footprints, collisions, how many lanes are worth it, waves, the coordinator and lane sessions.
intro: More lanes help only until the first limit is reached, the knee. Past it they add queues, tokens and collisions. In the testbed, ten lanes at once lasted about 15 minutes before the usage limit stopped them [M], while two at a time got further.

The ideas here decide before a wave starts which slices can run side by side, how many lanes are worth it and where they would collide. Since 13 November FixFlow’s ship plan runs a coordinator session with one lane session per phase, so this theme is moving from design into daily use.

tokens.title: Spend fewer tokens per result
tokens.covers: Where the tokens go and how to spend fewer: long windows, the fixed start of every agent, lookups, compaction, model tiers and one written budget.
intro: We counted every model call on this PC for both projects: 35,834 calls and 7.35 billion context tokens [M]. 97 % of those tokens were re-reads of a window the model had already read [M], so the number of calls times the size of the window is what we have to manage.

The ideas here are the four levers the token report found, the governor and the written budget of harness v2, and smaller habits that keep windows short. Each lever is sized as an exposure, the share of tokens it could touch, which tells us where to aim; the savings themselves are what the next measurements will show.

memory.title: Remember what we learned
memory.covers: Carrying what we learn from one session to the next: the knowledge store, the reasoning-cache library, lessons that become checks, staleness and privacy.
intro: Every new session starts without what the last one learned, unless something carries it across. The ideas here give the harness a memory: the knowledge store designed in PR #183, the reasoning-cache library of harness v2, and smaller habits such as turning a lesson into a check.

My goal for the library is that a cheaper model finishes more of our work at the same quality. The pathway map shows, step by step, where an entry can be lost before it helps, which tells us what to build first. Both designs are complete on paper and unproven so far; their first steps are cheap tests built to prove them.

retrieval.title: Find the right code fast
retrieval.covers: Finding what a change touches: indexes, the typed code store, graph engines, co-change, search baselines, touch lists and a what-is-true-now view.
intro: Before an agent can change code it has to find what the change touches. On 75 held-out FixFlow commits, a typed store of code facts put 0.700 of the touched files and definitions in front of the reader within an 8,000-token answer [M], ahead of a scripted search at 0.625 [M]. The gain sits in the mobile app; outside it the two are still too close to call.

The three engines we tried, one relational and two graph, gave identical answers, so the engine is a free choice. The test was a fixed script with no agent in it; the next step puts an agent in the loop and widens the test to knowledge graphs and caching, as I asked.

method.title: How we orchestrate
method.covers: How the main session plans, briefs and judges: model tiers, judgement-free discovery with citations, fresh-context checks, workflow shapes and recovery when an agent fails.
intro: Our method is written down in the orchestration design of 31 October: a main session that plans and judges, cheaper models that discover with citations, and fresh-context reviewers that try to refute what was found. This document was made that way.

The ideas here are how we brief agents, shape workflows, choose a model for each job and recover when an agent fails or returns nothing. Many are in use every day; the rest are refinements we have designed and can now test.

skills.title: Skills, agents and tools
skills.covers: Skill packages, saved project agents, tool lists and outside tools worth borrowing.
intro: A skill package teaches agents one domain; a project agent is a saved agent definition with its own model, tools and instructions. PR #185 holds 13 skill packages and 11 project agents for FixFlow.
The ideas here cover what to package, how to keep each agent’s fixed start small, how to know a skill is used, and which outside tools are worth borrowing.

measure.title: Measure, model and test ideas fairly
measure.covers: How we measure and test: transcript tallies, number tags, replays on recorded data, held-out protocols, system-dynamics and pathway models, and fair tests.
intro: Every number in this document carries a tag that says how sure we are of it. That habit, and most of the measurements in it, came from this theme.

The ideas here are how we measure and how we keep a test fair to the idea it tests: tallies from our own transcripts, replays on recorded work, held-out test sets frozen before the run, models of the whole system, and rules such as testing the strongest form of an idea against the strongest baseline.

release.title: First use, real devices and real hosts
release.covers: Finding last-day gaps on day one: zero-seed walks, rehearsals on a real host, load drills, Android builds, the emulator and the device lab.
intro: The clinic testbed’s last-day gaps were production paths hidden behind test data, and none of it had run on a real host. The ideas here find those gaps on day one: a walk from a clean install in every gate, a rehearsal on a real host, and a rerun of the load drill.
For FixFlow the same theme means real Android builds and real devices. The lab emulator already boots on this PC with Android 14 and the lab app installed.

owner.title: Owner-facing outputs and decisions
owner.covers: What reaches me: visual pages, decision boards, readability rules, notices and the standing rules that need my yes.
intro: I decide quickly when I can see the choice on one page. The ideas here shape what reaches me: visual pages I can read on my own screen, decision boards that show the options and what each one unblocks, and rules that keep anything reaching outside this PC behind my yes.
This document is one of them: one place where the whole team can see the ideas, the bottlenecks and the work.
